## Introduction

For this project, I worked with Melbourne housing data to predict house prices based on features such as the number of rooms, property type, distance and location. I used two models a regression tree and a random forest, to see which one gave better predictions. I then used the better performing model to build a prediction API..

## Data Preparation

The original dataset had 34857 rows and 21 columns. I selected seven predictors and used Price as the response variable. I removed rows with missing prices and converted categorical variables into factors. The cleaned dataset had 27247 rows.

```{r}

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

# Read the original data
housing <- read_csv("data/Melbourne_housing_FULL.csv")

# Keep variables for modeling
# Remove rows with missing prices
housing_model <- housing %>%
  select(Price, Rooms, Type, Distance,
         Bathroom, Car, Landsize, Regionname) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Price)) %>%
  mutate(
    Type = as.factor(Type),
    Regionname = as.factor(Regionname)
  )

# Check the cleaned data
dim(housing_model)
summary(housing_model)


```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

I used a histogram, boxplot and scatterplot to explore housing prices and see how they relate to property type and number of rooms.

```{r}
# Check the distribution of prices
ggplot(housing_model, aes(x = Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Housing Prices",
    x = "Price (AUD)",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Compare prices by property type
ggplot(housing_model, aes(x = Type, y = Price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Housing Prices by Property Type",
    x = "Property Type",
    y = "Price (AUD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Check rooms and price
ggplot(housing_model, aes(x = Rooms, y = Price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Rooms vs Housing Price",
    x = "Number of Rooms",
    y = "Price (AUD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The plots gave me a better understanding of how housing prices differ across properties. I also checked for missing values and found that some numeric variables had quite a few missing observations so I handled those during preprocessing.

```{r}
# Check missing values
housing_model %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))
```

## Model Training

I split the data into 70% training and 30% testing. I used 5-fold cross-validation to tune the models and median imputation to handle missing numeric values.

```{r}
# Load modeling packages
library(tidymodels)

# Split the data
set.seed(123)
housing_split <- initial_split(housing_model, prop = 0.70)

train_data <- training(housing_split)
test_data <- testing(housing_split)

# Check the sizes
dim(train_data)
dim(test_data)

# Create 5 folds
set.seed(123)
housing_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5)
housing_folds
```

```{r}
# Create a recipe
housing_recipe <- recipe(Price ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())

# Check the recipe
housing_recipe
```

### Regression Tree

I trained a regression tree using the rpart package. I tuned the tree depth and complexity parameter and selected the best model based on RMSE.

```{r}
# Create a regression tree
tree_model <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = 10
) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Check the model
tree_model
```

```{r}
# Create the tree workflow
tree_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(housing_recipe) %>%
  add_model(tree_model)

# Check the workflow
tree_workflow
```

```{r}
# Create tuning grid
tree_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(range = c(-4, -1)),
  tree_depth(range = c(2L, 10L)),
  levels = 4
)

# Check the grid
tree_grid
```

```{r}
# Tune the regression tree using 5-fold CV
set.seed(123)

tree_results <- tune_grid(
  tree_workflow,
  resamples = housing_folds,
  grid = tree_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

# Check tuning results
collect_metrics(tree_results)
```

```{r}
# Find the best tree using RMSE
best_tree <- select_best(tree_results, metric = "rmse")

# Check the best parameters
best_tree
```

```{r}
# Finalize the tree workflow
final_tree_workflow <- finalize_workflow(
  tree_workflow,
  best_tree
)

# Check the final workflow
final_tree_workflow
```

```{r}
# Fit the final tree on training data
final_tree_fit <- fit(final_tree_workflow, data = train_data)

# Predict prices for test data
tree_predictions <- predict(final_tree_fit, new_data = test_data) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data %>% select(Price))

# Check model performance
tree_metrics <- tree_predictions %>%
  metrics(truth = Price, estimate = .pred)

tree_metrics
```

### Random Forest

I trained a random forest model using 500 trees. I tried different values of mtry and min_n using 5-fold cross-validation. After finding the best combination based on RMSE, I trained the final model and checked its performance on the test data

```{r}
# Create a random forest model
rf_model <- rand_forest(
  mtry = tune(),
  trees = 500,
  min_n = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Check the model
rf_model
```

```{r}
# Create the random forest workflow
rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(housing_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_model)

# Check the workflow
rf_workflow
```

```{r}
# Create tuning grid for random forest
rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  mtry(range = c(2L, 7L)),
  min_n(range = c(5L, 20L)),
  levels = 3
)

# Check the tuning grid
rf_grid
```

```{r}
# Tune random forest using 5-fold CV
set.seed(123)

rf_results <- tune_grid(
  rf_workflow,
  resamples = housing_folds,
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq)
)

# Check tuning results
collect_metrics(rf_results)
```

```{r}
# Find the best random forest using RMSE
best_rf <- select_best(rf_results, metric = "rmse")

# Check the best parameters
best_rf
```

```{r}
# Finalize the random forest workflow
final_rf_workflow <- finalize_workflow(
  rf_workflow,
  best_rf
)

# Check the final workflow
final_rf_workflow
```

```{r}
# Fit the final random forest on training data
final_rf_fit <- fit(final_rf_workflow, data = train_data)

# Predict prices for test data
rf_predictions <- predict(final_rf_fit, new_data = test_data) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data %>% select(Price))

# Check model performance
rf_metrics <- rf_predictions %>%
  metrics(truth = Price, estimate = .pred)

rf_metrics
```

## Model Comparison

After training both models, I compared their performance using RMSE, R-squared and MAE. The random forest performed better than the regression tree because it had lower prediction errors and a higher R-squared value.

The random forest had an RMSE of about 325431 and an R-squared of 0.744. Based on these results, I decided to use the random forest as my final model.

```{r}
# Compare regression tree and random forest
model_comparison <- bind_rows(
  tree_metrics %>% mutate(Model = "Regression Tree"),
  rf_metrics %>% mutate(Model = "Random Forest")
) %>%
  select(Model, .metric, .estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = .metric,
    values_from = .estimate
  )

# Check comparison
model_comparison
```

```{r}
# Save the final random forest model
dir.create("models", showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(final_rf_fit, "models/random_forest_model.rds")

# Check that the model was saved
file.exists("models/random_forest_model.rds")
```

## Conclusion

After comparing both models, I found that the random forest gave better results than the regression tree. The random forest had a lower RMSE of 325431 compared to 361217 for the regression tree. It also had a higher Rsquared value of 0.744 and a lower MAE of 191576.

Since the random forest performed better I chose it as my final model and used it to create a Plumber API to predict housing prices. I also used Docker to package the API.
